Lebanon’s Nationwide Strike Paralyzes Commerce and Public Services

A sweeping general strike brought much of Lebanon’s economic activity to a halt on Thursday, as workers across multiple sectors demanded urgent government action on public sector wages and deteriorating living conditions. The coordinated walkout, led by major labor unions and professional associations, has shuttered banks, disrupted public transportation, and closed government offices in Beirut and major provincial cities.

With negotiations between union leaders and government officials ongoing, the strike shows no sign of abating. The Lebanese Federation of Trade Unions estimated that participation exceeded 60% across key sectors, including transport, banking, and education. Supermarkets, pharmacies, and retail outlets operated on limited hours or closed entirely as supply chains stalled.

Traffic was sparse in downtown Beirut, with public buses idled and taxi drivers joining picket lines. “We cannot continue working under these conditions,” said Samir Khalil, head of the National Transport Workers Union. “Our wages have lost all value, and prices keep rising.”

Banking operations were severely disrupted, with the Association of Lebanese Banks reporting over 80% of branches closed nationwide. ATM withdrawals were restricted in several areas. “The financial sector cannot function properly without stability and basic public services,” said Ziad Farhat, an economist at Levant Analytics.

Schools and universities suspended classes, while many government services, including passport issuance and utility bill processing, were temporarily halted. The Chamber of Commerce projected daily economic losses at up to $30 million, warning that prolonged disruption could further strain Lebanon’s fragile economy.

Prime Minister Fouad Mahmoud called for dialogue, urging unions to end the strike amid ongoing IMF negotiations. However, union leaders insisted that immediate relief was needed. “This strike is our last resort,” said Layla Haddad, spokesperson for the Unified Public Sector Union. “We will not return to work until our demands are addressed.”

Discussions between government officials and union representatives were continuing as the strike entered its second day.
